title: Regulatory Roadmap for Advancing Digital Trade Integration in Mercosur
location: The principal location is Buenos Aires, Argentina.
executive_summary: Mercosur has rapidly emerged as a digital leader in Latin America, with significant growth in ecommerce and digital startups. However, most digital trade remains domestic due to fragmented regulations across member countries. Key barriers include inconsistent rules on data privacy, intermediary liability, OTT services, taxation, and customs procedures, which particularly hinder SMEs’ ability to scale and export. Surveyed firms estimate that improving digital regulations could boost revenues and exports by nearly 30% annually. The report recommends harmonizing digital regulations, modernizing customs, fostering mutual recognition of online service providers, supporting SME skills and finance, and establishing a regional Digital Dialogue. By creating a coherent regional digital market, Mercosur can unlock substantial trade, investment, and job creation, ensuring its competitiveness in the global digital economy. Immediate, coordinated action is essential to fully realize these opportunities.
characteristics: Mercosur is a regional digital leader, with rapid growth in ecommerce and digital startups, but most digital trade remains domestic due to regulatory fragmentation.

Online sellers in Mercosur are more likely to export, export to multiple markets, and experience faster growth than offline firms; digital trade boosts SME participation in regional/global value chains.
Key barriers include inconsistent digital regulations (data privacy, OTT, liability, taxes), logistics/customs challenges, and limited access to finance, especially for SMEs.
Harmonizing digital regulations, modernizing customs, and fostering regional interoperability (e.g., payments, mutual recognition) could increase revenues/exports by ~30% annually.

Policy recommendations: adopt smart, interoperable digital regulations; create safe harbors; modernize copyright; avoid excessive digital taxes; improve logistics; and establish public-private digital dialogues and skills/finance programs for SMEs.

Political Actors: Information and Communication Technologies and Digital Dialogue Leaders
Economic Actors: Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean

practical_applications: Brazil’s Marco Civil da Internet (2014) includes a “safe harbor” provision that limits the responsibility of internet service providers for hosting or transferring third-party content.

Brazil’s data protection law, Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD), passed in 2018 and effective from 2020, requires companies to comply with strict requirements related to the processing of personal data, similar to the EU’s GDPR.
Uruguay’s free trade agreement with Chile includes a robust ecommerce chapter that respects free flow of data across borders and bars data localization requirements.
Argentina is in the process of concluding a similar free trade agreement with Chile, aiming for provisions that facilitate digital trade and data flows.
Uruguay has a data protection law (2008) and a 2013 resolution defining personal data and its treatment, requiring companies with .uy websites to register data and provide privacy policies.
Argentina’s Data Protection Law (2000) prohibits the transfer of personal data to countries lacking adequate protections, with ongoing updates to clarify international data transfer regimes.
Argentina introduced a 21 percent tax on domestic and offshore internet services in March 2018.
Uruguay implemented a 22 percent tax on online services such as Airbnb and Uber in January 2018.
Brazil’s National Cinema Agency has proposed regulations to tax audiovisual OTT platforms and require a minimum quota of Brazilian content, as well as investment in co-production of original content.
Brazil’s Apex export promotion agency has created training programs for SMEs to use ecommerce to export.
Chile’s export promotion agency ProChile offers comprehensive “Digital Exports” seminars on ecommerce, digital marketing, and international promotional campaigns.

Mexico’s export promotion agency Proméxico has organized seminars and training for SMEs, created a B2B platform for Mexican SMEs selling to overseas markets, and offers consulting services for digital marketing and online payments.
Costa Rica’s export promotion agency Procomer provides a one-stop access for B2C and B2B merchants to global platforms like I.Gourmet, Alibaba, and Amazon.

Latin America’s Exporta Fácil program has simplified customs clearance for SMEs for shipments typically weighing less than 30 kilograms and valued under US$5,000, though it is limited to postal systems.
Uruguay XXI’s Proexport+ program supports new and existing exporters with up to $40,000 for product development, market research, and trade show participation.

The Chile-Uruguay FTA (2016) includes provisions for interoperable electronic signatures, acceptance of electronically filed trade documents, cooperation on consumer protection online, and prohibits forced data localization except for legitimate public policy reasons.

The Pacific Alliance (Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru) has a cooperation agreement on ecommerce, a Digital Agenda for regional digital market integration, and public-private dialogues on the digital economy.
The European Union’s Digital Single Market initiative aims to harmonize digital regulations and enable online content portability across member states.

ASEAN’s ICT Masterplan 2020 focuses on digital transformation and building a single integrated market for the digital economy, with legislation on electronic transactions, cybercrime, consumer protection, and data privacy.

APEC’s Electronic Commerce Steering Group (ECSG) and Paperless Trading Subgroup promote legal, regulatory, and policy environments for ecommerce, and are implementing strategies for cross-border paperless trading by 2020.
APEC’s Data Privacy Pathfinder and Subgroup support cross-border flow of personal information and promote common data privacy approaches, including the Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) system.

The Air Cargo Advanced Screening program in the United States, piloted with major shippers, provides customs authorities with air cargo data prior to loading at foreign ports, serving as a model for data-driven customs risk management.
